title: Antiphase warmup exploration — lab notes
content:
Quick description:
Antiphase warmup = deliberately staggered/alternating cache priming across two correlated request cohorts so their KV/prefix caches don't collide at once. Hypothesis: flatten p95/p99 spikes during mixed short+long context workloads by avoiding synchronized cache churn.

Motivation / context:
- Seen repeated p99 spikes on mixed workloads during morning traffic surge (short chat queries + long summarization jobs).
- Traditional global priming (run warm requests) tends to create temporary contention on KV allocations and GPU memory, leading to short-lived latency cliffs.
- Idea: split warmup into two antiphase cohorts (A/B) that prime complementary context slices so that eviction/rehydration is spread across time.

Experiment goals:
1) Measure effect on p50/p95/p99 latencies under synthetic mixed traffic.
2) Check tail noise reduction while keeping steady-state throughput and token-cost within 5% overhead.
3) Observe KV cache hit-rate stability and eviction churn.

Setup details (run notebook + params):
- Binary: local-run/antiphase-driver v0.3 (see linked PR).
- Model: llm-opus-v1-medium (quantized int8 variant used in dedicated pool).
- GPU: a2-32 (NVIDIA A10G) equivalent in our internal sandbox.
- Batch settings: adaptive-batch with target latency 120ms (baseline), max batch 32, min batch 1.
- KV cache: size cap 6GB per instance, eviction LRU.
- Warm cohorts: A = short queries (avg tokens 24, 80% of requests), B = long jobs (avg 512 tokens, 20% of requests).
- Antiphase schedule: cohort A primes at t = 0s, 200s, 400s...; cohort B primes at t = 100s, 300s, 500s... i.e., 180–220s spaced windows.
- Arrival pattern: diurnal-surge emulator with Poisson + periodic microbursts (matches production sample from 2024-09). Peak QPS ~480, baseline ~120.
- Metric capture: per-request latency, serialize token throughput, kv_hit_rate, eviction_count, GPU mem usage sampled every 5s.
- Duration: 60 minutes per trial.

Baseline (no warm / synchronous warm) quick numbers (median of 3 runs):
- p50: 38 ms
- p95: 158 ms
- p99: 372 ms
- throughput (tokens/s): 11.8k
- kv_hit_rate: 0.63
- eviction_count (avg per 60m): 14k

Antiphase run (single run summary):
- p50: 40 ms (+2 ms)
- p95: 132 ms (-26 ms)
- p99: 221 ms (-151 ms)  <-- main win here, big reduction
- throughput (tokens/s): 11.6k (-1.7%)
- kv_hit_rate: 0.71 (+8%)
- eviction_count: 9.5k (-32%)

Observations / raw notes:
- p99 improvement is stable across 3 independent runs (range 200–235 ms).
- Reduced eviction_count lines up with higher kv_hit_rate; seems the antiphase schedule prevents synchronized cache thrashing during microbursts.
- Small throughput penalty (~1.5–2%) likely due to occasional mismatch where a request arrives for a context slice that isn't primed yet; system falls back to slower cold-path token generation.
- CPU-side queuing: no meaningful increase in queue depth; GPU mem usage slightly smoother (stddev down ~18%).
- During the Antiphase windows, observed a ~50s zone where long jobs touched hot-keys; because they are offset from short queries, short queries had fewer cache misses.

Charts (ASCII-ish) — p99 over sliding 5m windows (baseline vs antiphase):
Baseline:  [280  340  460  380  360  420  390  370  410  380]
Antiphase: [210  220  205  230  240  225  210  205  220  215]
(rough sequence: baseline jittery with spikes up to 460ms; antiphase stable ~200–240ms)

Failure modes / caveats:
- If cohorts are misidentified (e.g., long queries mis-bucketed into cohort A) benefit disappears. Need robust bucketing logic (heuristic: tokens>128 => B) but that's brittle for some clients that send mixed.
- For extremely heavy long-job loads (B > 40% traffic), antiphase loses utility; both groups sail into contest on KV. We should detect and disable antiphase when cohort ratio crosses threshold.
- Edge case: model variant warm memory layout changes (different quantization) might shift eviction dynamics; run quick calibration per-model.

Next experiments / action items:
- (Short) Implement dynamic cohort detector: simple rolling histogram on token lengths + confidence threshold; flip to single global warm if cohort imbalance > 40/60. (Owner: me)
- (Perf) Try shorter antiphase intervals (50s offset) to see if more fine-grained staggering helps (risk: too-frequent priming adds overhead). (Owner: Omar)
- (Safety) Add guard to not run antiphase during maintenance/GPU drain windows. (Owner: SRE)
- (Measure) Add tracer tag to warm requests so we can run A/B on real production shadow traffic for 6h. (Owner: Marta)
- (Policy) Explore integrating into canary-rollout logic in console so customers can opt-in. (Product sync needed)

Notes to self / heuristics distilled:
- Antiphase best for mixed short-majority + long-minority workloads during surges.
- Tune warm interval to be roughly half the observed cold-fill time for a KV slice (experimentally around 180–240s here).
- Always measure eviction_count and kv_hit_rate together; hit_rate alone can be misleading if cache shrinks.

Questions / unresolved:
- Does antiphase help when model sharding across 2 GPUs with shared KV routing? Need a small cluster run.
- Can we combine antiphase with prefix-level LRU protection (pin top-10 prefixes) for further tail wins?
- How does antiphase interact with batching heuristics that already bias for latency vs throughput?

Slack refs / links:
- #serving-runtime thread: slack.com/archives/C01234ABC/p164... (see thread on 2024-10-22)
- proto PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-experiments/pull/214

Quick conclusion (working):
Antiphase warmup shows promising tail-latency reduction (p99) for our mixed-workload emulator with a small throughput cost. It seems to reduce eviction bursts by spacing cache refills temporally. Worth pursuing a cautious, measurable shadow deploy on production-like traffic, plus building the cohort detector to avoid misclassification.

Todo immediate:
- Add simple cohort detector + toggle (WIP branch).
- Run cluster-level test (2x A10G) next week.
- Draft short note for product on opt-in flag and potential cost/benefit tradeoffs.

End of notes.
